Write a simple policy explaining how you create, store, rotate, revoke, and delete keys and certificates.
List all your keys and certificates in an inventory spreadsheet, including expiry dates.
Pick tools like a hardware security module or cloud service for key storage, and a monitoring tool for certificates.
Set up alerts for certificates expiring soon and schedule key rotations at least yearly.
Test the rotation and revocation processes once to make sure they work.
9.3.evidenceExample: A policy document outlining your full process for managing keys and certificates; an inventory list showing all certificates with expiry dates; log files proving keys were rotated; and a diagram or description of your secure storage setup like an HSM or vault.

keyManagementTool.label: Key Management Tool
keyManagementTool.meaning: The name of the software or hardware you use to securely store and manage encryption keys.
keyManagementTool.whereToFind: Ask your IT or cloud admin what system holds your important encryption keys.

certificateMonitoringTool.label: Certificate Monitoring Tool
certificateMonitoringTool.meaning: The tool that tracks your digital certificates and warns you before they expire.
certificateMonitoringTool.whereToFind: Ask your IT team what software scans for expiring SSL certificates on your websites or servers.

certExpiryAlertDays.label: Cert Expiry Alert Days
certExpiryAlertDays.meaning: Number of days before a certificate expires when you want to get an alert to renew it.
certExpiryAlertDays.whereToFind: Look in your certificate tool settings or ask IT when they start renewal reminders.

10.1.summary: Your company needs to create a clear policy that controls who gets access to what systems based on their job, using roles and strict rules like least privilege. You're done when you have a documented policy with role definitions, approval processes, and rules for reviews and privileged access, approved by management.
10.1.applicability: Every company in scope needs this; no one skips it because access control protects all sensitive data and systems.
10.1.quickTip: Start by listing 5-10 common jobs in your company, like 'HR Manager' or 'IT Support', and jot down what systems each should access.
10.1.implementationSteps:
Write a simple access control policy document explaining the rules.
Define standard roles based on job functions and list permissions for each.
Map every employee to their role and note the process for requesting exceptions.
Get your management board to review and approve the policy.
Set up a schedule to review all access rights at least once a year.
10.1.evidenceExample: A policy document showing your access control rules, role definitions with permissions assigned to each, a process for approving access requests, and how you handle privileged access.

accessModel.label: Access Control Model (RBAC, ABAC, or hybrid)
accessModel.meaning: This picks the main way your company organizes access: RBAC uses job roles, ABAC checks situations like time or device, or hybrid mixes both.
accessModel.whereToFind: Ask your IT lead what model fits your setup; most start with RBAC for simplicity.

reviewFrequency.label: Access Review Frequency (standard and privileged)
reviewFrequency.meaning: How often you check and update everyone's access rights, separately for normal and high-risk access.
reviewFrequency.example: annual for standard, quarterly for privileged
reviewFrequency.whereToFind: ORP.4.A4 recommends at least annual for standard accounts, quarterly for privileged.

deprovisioningSla.label: De-provisioning SLA (hours to revoke access after termination)
deprovisioningSla.meaning: The maximum time allowed to cut off access when someone leaves the company.
deprovisioningSla.whereToFind: Check your HR offboarding process; ORP.4.A6 requires prompt deactivation.

sharedAccountPolicy.label: Shared / Generic Account Policy
sharedAccountPolicy.meaning: Whether shared or generic accounts (like 'admin@' or 'info@') are allowed. ORP.4.A3 requires unique identifiers for every user.
sharedAccountPolicy.whereToFind: Check if any systems use shared logins; CIR 11.5.3 only allows them with documented justification.

authReviewCycle.label: Authentication methods review cycle (years)
authReviewCycle.meaning: How often you review whether your authentication methods are still appropriate and up to date.
authReviewCycle.whereToFind: CIR 11.6.4 requires periodic review of authentication procedures.

10.2.summary: For each asset in your inventory, document who owns it, how access is controlled, and how many privileged/admin accounts exist. This is where you apply your 10.1 access control policy to concrete systems. You're done when every asset has an owner, access method, and privileged account count documented.
10.2.applicability: Every company with IT assets needs this. It's the per-asset implementation of your access control policy from 10.1.
10.2.quickTip: Open your asset register and go asset by asset: who owns it, how do people log in, does it have admin accounts?
10.2.implementationSteps:
Review your asset inventory from RSK 2.2.
For each asset, assign an owner (the person accountable for access decisions).
Document how access is managed per asset (e.g., Entra ID RBAC, SSH keys, CyberArk, manual).
Count privileged/admin accounts per asset (root, admin, service accounts with elevated permissions).
Review and update when assets are added, changed, or retired.
10.2.evidenceExample: A table showing each asset with its owner, access management method, and count of privileged accounts. The platform generates this automatically from your per-asset assignments.

10.3.summary: Document your company-wide processes for managing user access throughout the employee lifecycle (joining, moving roles, leaving) and how you handle privileged/admin accounts. You're done when you've named your tools, defined background check scope, and identified your PAM approach.
10.3.applicability: Every company with employees needs JML processes; PAM tooling is needed if you have any admin or service accounts.
10.3.quickTip: Ask HR: 'What happens when someone starts or leaves?' Ask IT: 'What tool manages admin accounts?'
10.3.implementationSteps:
Document your joiner-mover-leaver process: onboarding checklist, role change procedure, offboarding steps.
Name the tool(s) used to track JML (HR system, ticketing, spreadsheet).
Define background check scope per CIR Art. 10 (all employees, security roles, management).
Name your PAM tool or approach for admin account management.
Get management approval for the documented processes.
10.3.evidenceExample: A document describing your JML process with checklists, your PAM tool configuration, and background check policy, uploaded as evidence or maintained in the platform's policy module.

jmlTool.label: JML Tool
jmlTool.meaning: The software or system your company uses to track the joiner-mover-leaver process.
jmlTool.example: Entra ID lifecycle workflows + ServiceNow HR integration
jmlTool.whereToFind: Check with HR for their employee management software and IT for their access tracking tool.

backgroundCheckScope.label: Background Check Scope
backgroundCheckScope.meaning: Which employees get background checks before receiving system access.
backgroundCheckScope.example: All employees (basic) + enhanced checks for admin/security roles
backgroundCheckScope.whereToFind: Look in your HR onboarding docs or ask your HR manager what they verify for new employees.

pamTool.label: PAM Tool
pamTool.meaning: The tool or approach for managing privileged/admin accounts (CIR 11.3, ORP.4.A15).
pamTool.whereToFind: Ask your IT security team; common options are CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Teleport, or Microsoft PIM.

10.4.summary: Prove you're doing periodic access reviews by documenting when the last review happened. The review cadence is set in your 10.1 policy. This requirement tracks that you're actually doing it. You're done when you have a date and evidence of your last review.
10.4.applicability: Every company needs periodic access reviews. CIR 11.2.3 requires documented reviews, ORP.4.A4 specifies at least annual.
10.4.quickTip: Ask your IT manager when they last checked user access lists and get that date.
10.4.implementationSteps:
Pull a list of all user accounts per system.
Check if each person still needs their current access level.
Remove excess permissions and disable unused accounts.
Document findings: who was reviewed, what changed, who approved.
Upload the review report as evidence.
10.4.evidenceExample: A review report or spreadsheet showing accounts checked, changes made, and sign-off from system owners.

lastAccessReviewDate.label: Last Access Review Date
lastAccessReviewDate.meaning: The date of your most recent full check of user permissions across systems.
lastAccessReviewDate.whereToFind: Check your IT team's records for the latest access review report.

11.1.summary: Your company must roll out multi-factor authentication (MFA) on accounts and systems, starting with the highest-risk ones like admin accounts. You're done when MFA covers most users and systems, you've tracked enrollment numbers, and any exceptions are documented with approvals.
11.1.applicability: All companies in scope need this, but small firms with few remote users can prioritize just admin accounts and VPN first while planning broader rollout.
11.1.quickTip: Talk to your IT team today: ask what MFA tools they already use or recommend, like Microsoft Authenticator or YubiKeys.
11.1.implementationSteps:
Pick an MFA tool that works with your main systems (email, VPN, cloud apps).
Prioritize rollout: enforce MFA on all admin accounts right away, then remote access, then everything else over 12 months.
Track who has enrolled and what percentage of users are covered; aim for high numbers on critical accounts.
Create a list of any systems that can't use MFA yet, explain why, list extra security steps, and get a manager to sign off with a 12-month review date.
Check enrollment numbers every 3 months and adjust as needed.
11.1.evidenceExample: Screenshots or reports from your MFA tool showing deployment status, enrollment percentages for users and admins, the methods in use, and a spreadsheet or document listing approved exceptions with reasons, controls, and sign-offs.

mfaTool.label: MFA Tool
mfaTool.meaning: The main software or hardware tool your company uses to provide multi-factor authentication.
mfaTool.example: Microsoft Authenticator app with FIDO2 keys for admins
mfaTool.whereToFind: Ask your IT or security team what MFA solution they deployed or plan to use.

mfaMethods.label: MFA Methods
mfaMethods.meaning: The specific ways users prove their identity beyond password, like app codes or hardware keys.
mfaMethods.example: Authenticator app push notifications, hardware security keys
mfaMethods.whereToFind: Check your IT team's MFA setup docs or ask what options employees use to log in.

mfaCoverage.label: MFA Coverage
mfaCoverage.meaning: Which groups or systems have MFA turned on.
mfaCoverage.whereToFind: Review IT reports on where MFA is enforced, like just VPN or all user accounts.

mfaCoveragePct.label: MFA Coverage Pct
mfaCoveragePct.meaning: The percentage of users or accounts that are enrolled in and using MFA.
mfaCoveragePct.whereToFind: Get the latest enrollment report from your MFA tool's dashboard or IT team.

adminMfaEnforced.label: Admin MFA Enforced
adminMfaEnforced.meaning: Whether MFA is required with no exceptions for administrator or privileged accounts.
adminMfaEnforced.whereToFind: Confirm with IT if admin logins always require a second factor; it should be yes.

11.2.summary: Your company needs to set rules for using secure communication tools based on how sensitive the information is, ban personal apps for work data, and create a plan for communicating during emergencies like IT outages. You'll know you're done when you have a written policy, proof of approved encrypted tools, and records of testing your emergency channels.
11.2.applicability: Every company handling sensitive customer data under BSIG needs this; smaller firms without IT crises or sensitive comms might simplify it.
11.2.quickTip: List out what tools your team uses today for emails, chats, and calls, then decide which ones are safe for confidential info.
11.2.implementationSteps:
Write a short policy naming which tools to use for normal work (like encrypted email for confidential stuff) and banning personal apps like WhatsApp for business.
Pick and set up end-to-end encrypted tools like Signal for crises, and pre-make group chats for your crisis team and management board.
Create an emergency plan: pick main channel (e.g., Signal), backup (e.g., personal encrypted phones), and offline option (printed contacts), plus how to activate it.
Test the emergency channels with a quick drill, like sending a test message to the team.
Get your management board to review and approve the policy and plan.
11.2.evidenceExample: A policy document listing approved secure tools by data sensitivity level, proof like screenshots or setup guides showing end-to-end encrypted tools are deployed and configured, and a plan detailing emergency communication channels, procedures, and test records.

secureCommsTools.label: Secure Comms Tools
secureCommsTools.meaning: List the approved tools or methods for secure communication, matched to how sensitive the data is (like public, confidential, or top secret).
secureCommsTools.example: Confidential: Outlook with encryption + Signal; Strictly Confidential: Signal only or in-person meetings.
secureCommsTools.whereToFind: Ask your IT team what tools they currently use and recommend, or check what your data protection officer says fits your data levels.

emergencyCommsChannel.label: Emergency Comms Channel
emergencyCommsChannel.meaning: Name your main communication method for crises when normal IT systems are down.
emergencyCommsChannel.example: Signal group chat for crisis team.
emergencyCommsChannel.whereToFind: Decide this with your IT lead and management board based on what works without internet or company servers.

lastEmergencyCommsTest.label: Last Emergency Comms Test
lastEmergencyCommsTest.meaning: Date of your most recent test of the emergency communication setup.
lastEmergencyCommsTest.whereToFind: Check your IT team's calendar, meeting notes, or test logs for the latest drill.

11.3.summary: Your company needs to check all login methods and password rules against trusted security standards, then document the review and write a clear password policy. You're done when you have a review report confirming compliance and a policy everyone can follow.
11.3.applicability: Every company must do this if they have any digital logins for employees, customers, or systems; tiny companies with only paper processes can skip it.
11.3.quickTip: Ask your IT team for a list of all tools and apps where people log in. That's your starting point.
11.3.implementationSteps:
Ask your IT lead to review all login methods against BSI TR-03107 and NIST SP 800-63B standards, noting any issues like weak passwords or long sessions.
Write a simple password policy: set minimum length, lockouts after failed tries, and checks against leaked passwords.
Test session timeouts by leaving a login open and confirming it locks after your set time.
Get management to approve the review report and policy in a meeting.
Upload the review report and policy as proof.
11.3.evidenceExample: A review report that lists all authentication methods checked against BSI TR-03107 and NIST SP 800-63B, plus your written password policy showing rules like minimum length and lockouts.

ssoTool.label: Sso Tool
ssoTool.meaning: Name of any single sign-on tool your company uses for centralized logins across apps.
ssoTool.whereToFind: Ask your IT or security team what tool handles company-wide logins.

passwordMinLength.label: Password Min Length
passwordMinLength.meaning: The shortest number of characters allowed in any password across your systems.
passwordMinLength.whereToFind: Check your current IT password rules or ask your sysadmin what the minimum is set to now.

sessionTimeoutMinutes.label: Session Timeout Minutes
sessionTimeoutMinutes.meaning: How many minutes a login session stays active before it forces re-login for security.
sessionTimeoutMinutes.whereToFind: Look in your app or system's security settings, or ask IT how long sessions last before timeout.

12.1.summary: Figure out if your company falls under NIS2 rules by checking your sector and size, then classify it as essential, important, or required. You're done when you have a written document explaining your classification with legal reasons.
12.1.applicability: Managers at companies in key sectors like energy, transport, or health with 50+ employees or certain revenue need this; smaller companies outside those sectors can skip it.
12.1.quickTip: List what your company does and check if it matches the critical sectors in NIS2 Annex I or II.
12.1.implementationSteps:
List the sectors your company works in, like energy or banking.
Check your employee count and revenue against the thresholds: 250+ employees or €50M+ revenue for essential, 50+ for important.
Pick your classification: essential (high risk), important (medium risk), or required (special cases).
Write a short document explaining your sector, size, why you chose that class, and cite §28 BSIG.
Get your legal team or external lawyer to review it if unsure.
12.1.evidenceExample: A document that lists your company's sectors, employee count, revenue, chosen classification, and legal reasons why it fits under §28 BSIG.

entityClassification.label: Entity Classification
entityClassification.meaning: This picks your company's risk level under NIS2, which sets your reporting and supervision rules.
entityClassification.whereToFind: Compare your size and sector to BSIG §28 thresholds with your HR for employee numbers and finance for revenue.

applicableSectors.label: Applicable Sectors
applicableSectors.meaning: List the NIS2 sectors your business activities fall into from Annexes I or II.
applicableSectors.whereToFind: Review what your company does from management board discussions, annual reports, or business plans.

12.2.summary: Your company must register with Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) through their online portal to report critical IT operations. You're done when you get a confirmation with a registration number and upload proof of full registration.
12.2.applicability: Companies in Germany that run critical infrastructure services like energy, water, health, or transport must register; smaller non-critical businesses can skip this.
12.2.quickTip: Go to the BSI website and start setting up a 'Mein Unternehmenskonto' (MUK) account today. It takes weeks to get the digital certificate needed.
12.2.implementationSteps:
Set up a MUK account on the BSI portal with an ELSTER certificate; add at least two people who can access it.
Gather your company details like name, legal form, 24/7 contact person, IP address ranges, sector, and services.
Submit the full registration form including company size and countries you operate in.
Save the confirmation email or document with your BSI registration number.
Upload the proof to your compliance platform.
12.2.evidenceExample: A confirmation document or screenshot from BSI showing your registration number, submission date, and that all required company data was successfully submitted.

mukAccountId.label: Muk Account Id
mukAccountId.meaning: This is the unique ID for your company's Mein Unternehmenskonto (MUK) account used to access BSI services.
mukAccountId.whereToFind: In the confirmation email when you set up the MUK account or in the account dashboard on the BSI portal.

bsiRegistrationDate.label: Bsi Registration Date
bsiRegistrationDate.meaning: The date when BSI confirmed your full registration submission.
bsiRegistrationDate.whereToFind: On the BSI confirmation document, email, or in your MUK account under registration history.

registrationProofUploaded.label: Registration Proof Uploaded
registrationProofUploaded.meaning: The file upload spot for your BSI registration confirmation.
registrationProofUploaded.example: PDF of BSI confirmation showing registration number and complete data submission.
registrationProofUploaded.whereToFind: Download from your MUK account or email from BSI after successful registration.

12.3.summary: Keep your company's BSI registration info up to date by reviewing it every year and notifying them of changes within two weeks. You're done when you have records of your latest review, any change notifications with BSI confirmations, and proof your 24/7 contact person works with a backup.
12.3.applicability: Every German critical infrastructure company registered with the BSI must do this; smaller non-critical companies skip it.
12.3.quickTip: Log into your BSI account today and check if the contact person's details are still correct.
12.3.implementationSteps:
Assign a main contact person and a backup who can be reached anytime, day or night.
Review all registration details once a year. Check names, emails, IP ranges, services, and company info.
Update anything outdated right away and notify BSI within two weeks, saving their confirmation.
Document each review and change with the date and what you did.
Test that your contact person and backup respond quickly to ensure 24/7 availability.
12.3.evidenceExample: A dated note or meeting summary from your annual review showing you checked all fields and made updates if needed, plus emails or confirmations from BSI for any changes sent, and a simple test log proving your contact person and deputy are reachable anytime.

contactPersonName.label: Contact Person Name
contactPersonName.meaning: The full name of the person at your company who the BSI contacts about security issues and must be reachable 24/7.
contactPersonName.whereToFind: Your current BSI registration account or ask your IT/security lead who handles BSI communications.

contactPersonEmail.label: Contact Person Email
contactPersonEmail.meaning: The email address where BSI sends urgent security notifications to your designated contact person.
contactPersonEmail.whereToFind: Your BSI registration portal login or your company's security contact list.

lastRegistrationUpdate.label: Last Registration Update
lastRegistrationUpdate.meaning: The date when you last reviewed and updated your BSI registration details.
lastRegistrationUpdate.whereToFind: Check your BSI account history, emails from BSI confirmations, or your internal review notes.

nextRegistrationUpdate.label: Next Registration Update
nextRegistrationUpdate.meaning: The planned date for your next full annual review of the BSI registration.
nextRegistrationUpdate.whereToFind: Set this one year after your last update, based on your company's annual compliance calendar.

12.4.summary: Your company needs to organize key security documents into a ready-to-share catalog and set up a process to quickly respond to government requests from BSI. You're done when you have a document list, a named person to handle replies, a log of any past correspondence, and extra details if you're a critical infrastructure operator.
12.4.applicability: Every German company needs this to meet BSIG laws; critical infrastructure operators (KRITIS) have extra steps like submitting facility data.
12.4.quickTip: List out all your security docs like risk assessments and training records on a simple spreadsheet. That's your starting catalog.
12.4.implementationSteps:
Name one person (like your compliance or IT lead) responsible for handling BSI requests, and set a goal like 'reply within 48 hours'.
Make a catalog listing your key documents: security policies, risk assessments, incident logs, audits, and training proofs.
Write a short process: how you'll gather and send docs when BSI asks.
If you're KRITIS, add your facility details, capacities, and attack detection setup proofs to the catalog.
Start a log for any BSI emails or calls, even if none yet.
12.4.evidenceExample: A document or spreadsheet catalog listing your security documents with descriptions and locations, plus a one-page process description naming the responsible person and response times; for KRITIS, include facility data sheets or attack detection confirmations.

informationSharingCompliant.label: Information Sharing Compliant
informationSharingCompliant.meaning: Describe how your company is set up to share security info with BSI quickly and completely.
informationSharingCompliant.example: We have a catalog of 20+ security documents ready to share. Compliance officer replies to BSI within 24 hours. Log tracks all requests.
informationSharingCompliant.whereToFind: Ask your compliance or legal team, or check recent IT/security meeting notes.

correspondenceLogUploaded.label: Correspondence Log Uploaded
correspondenceLogUploaded.meaning: Upload any file tracking past communications with BSI or government regulators about security.
correspondenceLogUploaded.example: A simple Excel sheet with columns for date, sender, topic (e.g. 'BSI info request on incidents'), and response sent.
correspondenceLogUploaded.whereToFind: Check emails or shared drives in legal, compliance, or IT departments for BSI-related correspondence.
